items.text: Secure Access Service Edge, commonly called SASE, is a network architecture that provides secure access to cloud-based applications, services, and data from anywhere, at any time, and on any device. Gartner introduced the concept of SASE in 2019 as a response to the growing need for a more comprehensive and unified approach to network security. This approach simplifies network management, improves security, and enhances user experience by offering a unified and consistent security policy across all devices and locations.

Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) investigate and responds to cyber incidents such as data breaches, network intrusions, and malware attacks. It involves collecting and analyzing digital evidence to identify the scope of the incident, contain it, and recover from it. DFIR includes various techniques and tools such as forensic imaging, malware analysis, network analysis, and log analysis. DFIR aims to minimize the damage caused by cyber incidents and prevent them from recurring.

children.text: Approach & Methodologies

items.text: Identification: This involves identifying the scope of the incident, the affected assets, and the potential impact of the incident.
Collection: This involves the collection of evidence, such as network logs, system images, and other relevant data.
Preservation: This involves preserving the integrity of the evidence collected by following proper chain of custody procedures.
Analysis: This involves analyzing the collected evidence to identify the incident' s cause and extent and determine the best course of action.
Reporting: This involves preparing a comprehensive report of the findings and recommendations for the future prevention of similar incidents.
Remediation: This involves taking steps to mitigate the incident' s impact and prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future
Legal: This involves ensuring that all legal requirements and obligations are met during the investigation and reporting phases, including compliance with data privacy and security laws.

image.alt: Digital forensics process diagram: identification, collection, preservation, analysis, reporting, remediation and legal

children.text: Types of DFIR Services

items.text: Network Forensics: Investigation of network traffic to identify potential security breaches, malware infections, or other unauthorized activities.

items.text: Penetration Testing, aka Pen Testing, is a simulation of a real-world cyber-attack. Penetration Testing-as-a-Service helps you discover the weaknesses in your IT infrastructure by simulating an attack on a computer system or network from external and internal threats. The difference between a real attack and simulation of a real-world cyber-attack is that a real attack vanishes your business within minutes. Still, Penetration Testing attacks find vulnerabilities in a controlled system, helping you discover and fix problems before an attacker does. The output is a comprehensive report identifying where to close security holes and how to improve security posture.

children.text: Every Business Depends on Data Backup Solutions

Data has become the most valuable asset any business can have. In an increasingly digital business environment, companies rely on computers to process client information, payrolls, contracts, business plans, and more.

Most of this data is either critical to your business operations or contains sensitive, confidential information — or both. It’s no wonder, then, that companies go to great lengths to keep their data safe.

image.alt: Illustration of an IT technician working on servers and a laptop

children.text: It’s a different story for small- and medium-sized businesses. Installing and maintaining backup appliances and solutions is expensive, and many SMB budgets can’t stretch far enough to ensure reliable backup.

These numbers highlight one simple fact. Every business, no matter their industry, requires powerful enterprise backup services to protect themselves and their clients and customers.
Here we’ll explore the most effective backup solutions for small businesses, how they work, and how your operation can best employ them.
Local or Cloud Backup — Which to Choose?
In general, companies have two options available for them when they want to backup data. They can do it either locally, or choose to upload their backups to cloud storage.
Let’s take a closer look at both solution and how they protect data.

children.title: Local Backups
children.description: Local, or on premises, backup uses data storage media that's directly plugged into your system, such as external hard drives or physical servers. These kinds of devices are generally known as direct-attached storage, or DAS. There are certain benefits to keeping your backups on premises. DAS devices aren't connected to the internet and are stored in-house, meaning that no third party can access your files. They also give you, their owner, complete physical control over the storage devices. However, the on-site location means that your backup drives are vulnerable to any physical disaster that takes place at your office. You will also need to hire a dedicated IT team to maintain and manage data on your DAS devices, which can be extremely expensive. Finally, there are no guarantees on uptime or recovery time with physical in-house devices.

children.title: Cloud Backups
children.description: Cloud backup solutions store your data off-site at a data center owned by a third party. Generally, the backups are handled by a backup software that often function automatically to push your data to the server. Cloud backup has several advantages over local backups. The backup and recovery software generally supports both computers and mobile devices, enabling users to access and recover data both in the office and at a remote site. A cloud-based enterprise backup solution will also ensure data availability at all times, significantly cutting downtime in the event of data loss. Most cloud backup service providers also offer data integrity and recovery assurance, which provides clear business value by protecting your operational continuity.

children.title: Local or Cloud?
children.description: So, should you choose a local or cloud backup solution? The answer might surprise you — you need both. To properly protect your entire system, you must have a comprehensive backup plan that includes both on- and off-site data protection. Local solutions are often small-scale and not fit for businesses, while relying only on cloud solutions means you can't access your company's data without the internet. A complete enterprise backup and disaster recovery strategy ensures you'll have the best of both worlds.

children.text: Best Practices in Data Protection
Now that we know your business requires both local and cloud storage, the question is how do you actually use them? To properly protect and restore data, use these industry best practices.

One fact of IT is that, eventually, every single system will break or fail — often without warning. If you don’t backup your files on a regular basis, you risk significant loss of data when hardware failure happens.
At the very least, you should backup your data once every week. However, shorter 24-hour intervals are recommended.
To completely safeguard your business from data loss and hardware failure, remember these numbers: 3-2-1. A
3-2-1 backup plan
means you maintain three copies of data, two on separate local storage devices, and one on a cloud server.

This approach helps you avoid a single point of failure if disaster strikes. If your local drives break, you can access your cloud backup copy — if the cloud becomes unavailable, your data is still safe on-site.
If you manage all your backup processes manually, it’s all too easy to forget to do it. This brings us back to introducing unnecessary vulnerability to your infrastructure.
The best approach is to use an automated backup solution. This way you can work in peace knowing that you’re always on the ball with backup and recovery.
It’s not enough to only backup some data. A partial backup and recovery solution only opens the door for possible data losses.

Make sure that your data protection strategy encompasses your entire environment, including all mobile endpoints. Use data compression and encryption to make your information more manageable and to keep it safe.
